section_summary: This section begins with a Lima Embassy report on the Japanese population of South America and then contains a large group of September 1942 Radio Tokyo Spanish-language broadcasts aimed at Latin America. The broadcasts combine wartime news, Axis propaganda, criticism of Roosevelt and Britain, praise for Japanese rule and Manchukuo, allegations about the treatment of Japanese Americans, and appeals to Argentine and Chilean neutrality. The final documents concern intercepted Japanese correspondence in Argentina, Japanese propaganda and intelligence networks involving strategic minerals, the movements of Chilean deputies Rafael Moreno Echavarría and Pedro García de la Huerta, and U.S. monitoring of Moreno.

subfiles.title: Japanese Population in South America
subfiles.from: Rolland Welch, for the U.S. Ambassador, American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese population figures for South America and translates an article by Japanese attaché Shin-ichi Yokoyama.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reproduces Japanese Central Society of Peru statistics showing 225,005 Japan-born residents in the Americas listed, overwhelmingly concentrated in Brazil and Peru, and separately estimates Peru's Japanese and Nisei population. It considers the Peruvian figures reasonably accurate. A translated article by Shin-ichi Yokoyama describes Japanese commercial and agricultural activity and envisions later generations linking Japanese communities across the Andes and Amazon region.

subfiles.title: ONI request for Lima despatches 4991 and 4890
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of the American Republics, Liaison Office
subfiles.to: Department of State officials handling American Republics and Far Eastern distribution
subfiles.about: Requests copies of two Lima despatches for the Far Eastern Section of the Office of Naval Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: The Liaison Office reports that ONI's Far Eastern Section wants Lima despatches 4991 and 4890 concerning the Japanese situation in South America. It also asks that comparable future reports be supplied in duplicate so both ONI and the American Republics Section can retain copies.

subfiles.title: Distribution of Lima despatch 4991
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Transmits the Lima report on the Japanese population of South America to U.S. intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department circulates a copy of strictly confidential despatch 4991 of September 28, 1942. The recipients are Army military intelligence, naval intelligence, and the FBI.

subfiles.title: Radio broadcasts from Japan to Latin America
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards confidentially obtained interceptions of Japanese broadcasts directed to Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The FBI director sends Berle copies of Radio Tokyo broadcasts intercepted by a reliable confidential source. The same material was also being supplied to the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast to Latin America: Korea and Allied criticism
subfiles.about: Presents anti-Allied news items and a lecture praising Japanese administration and development in Korea.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast attacks the United States and Britain, praises Japanese administration in Java, condemns the Atlantic Charter, and alleges large British naval losses. A lecture by Iwasaki gives a tendentious history of Korea and credits Japan with reviving Korean industry, agriculture, education, and public life. The transcript is incomplete and heavily affected by a noisy recording.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast to Latin America, September 9
subfiles.about: Uses reports about the Pacific war, India, Europe, and the U.S. economy to portray the Allies as militarily and politically collapsing.
subfiles.summary: News items claim severe American naval losses, continuing revolt in India, threatened destruction of the Soviet Black Sea fleet, disorder in Northern Ireland, and Japanese administrative achievements in Asia. The broadcast also accuses American authorities of cruelty toward detained Japanese civilians. Iwasaki's concluding commentary presents Roosevelt's anti-inflation program as proof of dictatorship and impending American economic disaster.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast to Latin America, September 11
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese claims from Burma, the Philippines, Manchukuo, and Madagascar in a badly recorded broadcast.
subfiles.summary: The surviving items mention fighting near Akyab, the release of Philippine prisoners, a Manchukuo census, and alleged mistreatment of Japanese in San Pedro. Further reports discuss Australian supply problems and the British invasion of Madagascar. The translator notes that the recording is extremely poor and that several records were accidentally peeled before translation.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast to South America: Roosevelt and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Attacks American internment, British rule in India and Egypt, and Roosevelt's economic program while praising Manchukuo and Japanese wartime organization.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast alleges inhumane American treatment of 13,000 Japanese residents, unrest in India, British pressure on Egypt, and shortages of trained American naval personnel. It celebrates Manchukuo's anniversary, reports supplies moving into North China, and praises industrial activity in the Philippines. A lengthy commentary quotes Roosevelt's economic warnings and depicts his request for price-control powers as evidence of dictatorship and national collapse.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast to Latin America, September 14
subfiles.about: Marks Manchukuo's anniversary and presents Axis-favorable reports from India, Europe, the Soviet front, Southeast Asia, and the Caribbean.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast praises Manchukuo, condemns Britain's attack on Madagascar, and reports continuing Indian resistance and Hindu and Muslim cooperation. It claims successful German advances at Stalingrad, Turkish rejection of Willkie's proposal, Japanese agricultural development in Celebes, and disunity between British and American forces in Egypt. It concludes with reports of British paper shortages and an Axis submarine attack at Carlisle Bay, Barbados.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast to Central and South America, September 15
subfiles.to: Radio listeners in Central and South America
subfiles.about: Combines allegations about mistreatment of Japanese Americans with attacks on U.S. economic, military, and diplomatic credibility.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast describes alleged abuse and dispossession of Japanese detainees in Arizona and Missoula, warns of American inflation, and belittles the Allied supply route to Chiang Kai-shek. It cites Chungking criticism of American victory claims and Life photographs of Dutch Harbor damage, then reports an Indian factory strike, Ambassador Steinhardt's departure from Turkey, failed Allied landings, and attacks on hospital ships. It ends by quoting Sir Robert Craigie on Japanese wartime organization and celebrating Manchukuo's economic growth.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast to Latin America, September 16
subfiles.about: Celebrates Japan's air attack on Oregon and portrays U.S. policy in the Pacific and Latin America as weak, deceptive, and imperialistic.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast claims that the Oregon bombing exposed the defenselessness of the continental United States, mocks Willkie's Turkish mission, and criticizes U.S. arms production, naval reporting, and impending conscription of married men. Other items concern Chiang Kai-shek, Canadian wheat for the Soviet Union, fighting in New Guinea, Allied planning for India, and Manchukuo's development. Iwasaki's concluding lecture calls U.S. bases in the Galápagos an imperial seizure intended to dominate Ecuador, Peru, Chile, and the rest of Latin America.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast and Chilean independence program, September 17
subfiles.to: Radio listeners in Latin America, especially Chile
subfiles.about: Reports wartime news and then presents a special program praising Chilean neutrality on its independence anniversary.
subfiles.summary: The news portion announces Masayuki Tani's appointment as foreign minister, depicts Japanese attacks as spreading terror in the United States, and criticizes U.S. arms-loan negotiations with Argentina and Chile. It praises Argentine neutrality, discusses the delayed American admission of Yorktown's loss, British shortages, Iran oil, India, Stalingrad, and scarcity in Chungking territory. The Chilean anniversary program features Eiji Kawasaki and Gustavo Labarca Garas praising Chilean independence, neutrality, national character, and friendship with Japan.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo Spanish broadcast: Philippines, Iraq, Tōgō, and South America
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese administrative claims in the Philippines and Asia before concluding with a partially recorded commentary praising former foreign minister Tōgō.
subfiles.summary: News items concern the treatment of former Philippine soldiers, Manila's population, the removal of Singapore's founder's statue, production obstacles in India, Soviet weakness, British policy in Iraq, and revolt in Northern Ireland. The recording of Iwasaki's lecture begins in mid-speech because the operator failed to start the recorder. The surviving portion praises Tōgō's agreements with French Indochina and Thailand, his efforts to preserve relations with Chile, Brazil, Peru, and Argentina, and the supposed unity of the Japanese government.

subfiles.title: Forwarding of film of Japanese correspondence
subfiles.doc_type: Embassy despatch and Central Information Office report
subfiles.about: Forwards microfilm of Japanese correspondence secretly supplied by an Argentine contact and asks whether the surveillance should continue.
subfiles.summary: An Argentine contact had been asked by a local Japanese firm to act as an intermediary for correspondence moving among several American republics. Because the Embassy could not translate the material or determine whether it was harmless, it forwarded a developed roll of film to Washington. Pending instructions, the contact would continue accepting the correspondence and the Embassy would continue photographing it.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese correspondence film to the FBI
subfiles.about: Sends the Buenos Aires correspondence film and requests advice for answering the Embassy.
subfiles.summary: The Department transmits the Buenos Aires despatch and its original film enclosure to the FBI. It asks for an appropriate response concerning whether the Embassy should continue photographing and submitting the correspondence.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Gordon Reid concerning Japanese activities in South America
subfiles.to: Department of State files and officials
subfiles.about: Records Gordon Reid's allegations concerning Japanese-directed mineral smuggling, propaganda, agents, and population movements in South America.
subfiles.summary: Reid described investigations into Japanese-directed tungsten smuggling from mines owned by Mr. Williams and credited Francis Herron with helping expose the activity. He identified former Japanese naval officer Ko Nagasawa in Lima, described anti-U.S. propaganda distribution in Argentina by Pugnalin, and reported an unnamed Eurasian shipping expert who allegedly managed a continent-wide intelligence and funding network. He also accused the Swiss-German Mr. Bye of acquiring Chilean copper and cobalt mines for Japanese interests and reported Japanese movement from Brazil through Paraguay into the mining regions of Bolivia, Argentina, and Chile.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Gordon Reid memorandum to Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Encloses the October 1 Hiss-Reid memorandum for the Embassy's strictly confidential information.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State sends the Buenos Aires Embassy a copy of the memorandum recording Alger Hiss's conversation with Gordon Reid. The document is expressly classified strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Visits of Chilean deputies Rafael Moreno and Pedro García de la Huerta to Brazil
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports the August and September travel of two Chilean deputies in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo.
subfiles.summary: Rafael Moreno visited Rio de Janeiro in late August and São Paulo in early September, ostensibly to attend a Eucharistic Congress. Pedro García de la Huerta visited Rio in August as part of a Santiago Jockey Club delegation attending the Rio Jockey Club Grand Prix.

subfiles.title: Forwarding Rio telegram 4625 to Santiago
subfiles.about: Forwards the Rio Embassy's report on the Brazilian visits of the Chilean deputies.
subfiles.summary: The Department instructs the recipient embassy to take up Rio de Janeiro telegram 4625 of November 8. The document is marked confidential and intended to relay the travel information concerning the Chilean deputies.

subfiles.title: Rafael Moreno Echavarría surveillance update
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of the American Republics
subfiles.to: Mr. Chapin; Mr. Deniel; Mr. Bonsal
subfiles.about: Reports Moreno's arrival in Miami and arrangements for the FBI to monitor him.
subfiles.summary: The FBI reported that Moreno arrived in Miami from Panama on November 24 and would remain briefly before coming to the Embassy in Washington. Arrangements had been made to keep him under surveillance while there. Because the FBI did not handle his Panama stay, reports from Army and Navy intelligence were still awaited.

subfiles.title: Rio reply concerning Rafael Moreno
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Replies that the Rio Embassy has no adverse record concerning Rafael Moreno's activities in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Responding to the Department's inquiry about Deputy Rafael Moreno, the Rio Embassy states that it has no adverse record of his activities there. The terse reply is marked for close paraphrase before disclosure.
